top_choice_rationale: P003 (Melitz and Helpman, firm heterogeneity and selection) is the contribution I judge best established. It changed the welfare accounting of trade liberalisation and the structure of quantitative trade models, and it has faced dense firm-level testing for two decades. The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus foreign direct investment broadens it beyond the 2003 paper. Part of the empirical support fits facts that predate the theory, so I do not treat it as out-of-sample confirmation. The main weakness is attribution: Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not credited, and I would word the citation narrowly around selection, exporting versus foreign direct investment, and the gains from trade. P001 (Grossman and Helpman, political economy of trade protection) is a close second. It has the cleanest two-name credit, its core work is about thirty years old, and it is serious and mature, but its empirical support is mixed and specification-sensitive. I would support it with a citation confined to trade-policy political economy and making no claim of empirical validation. P002 (Autor, Dorn and Hanson) is strong design-based work with a stable three-name set. The long-run persistence of its effects and the shift-share identification debate are still being revised, and the task-framework antecedents are uncredited. P000 is last because at least two proposals describe prize-worthy discoveries. This ranking is by merit, attribution and maturity, not by the number of supporters.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile. I have no documented collaboration or institutional tie with Melitz, Helpman, Grossman, Autor, Dorn or Hanson. I held Harvard-based positions from 2006 to 2017, and some credited persons may be Harvard-affiliated. I have not verified this and it is not a documented personal connection. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
